```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5
)
# The classification section uses a suggested package
has_penguins <- requireNamespace("palmerpenguins", quietly = TRUE)
# The plots use the suggested packages glex, ggplot2 and patchwork
has_glex <- all(vapply(c("glex", "ggplot2", "patchwork"), requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE))
site <- "https://plantedml.com/randomPlantedForest/articles/"
```

`randomPlantedForest` implements Random Planted Forest ([Hiabu, Mammen & Meyer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.14563)), a tree ensemble whose predictions you can read off directly.
The fitted model is a short sum of main effects and interactions: these components add up exactly to the prediction, so the explanation is exact and not a post-hoc approximation, and each component can be plotted on its own.
Interactions of three predictors are simplified such that each can be displayed as the sum of a limited number (`max_panels`) of heat maps.

This guide fits a model, prints it, predicts with it and reads its components.

```{r setup}
library(randomPlantedForest)
```

## A first model

To see what the model recovers, we simulate data whose components are known.
The outcome depends on `x1`, `x2` and `x3` through main effects of different shapes, and on `x1` and `x2` jointly through a product; `x4` has no effect:

$$y = 1 + \sin(\pi x_1) + 2\left(x_2^2 - \tfrac{1}{3}\right) + \tfrac{x_3}{2} + 2 x_1 x_2 + \varepsilon$$

```{r simulate}
set.seed(1)
n <- 1000
sim <- data.frame(
  x1 = runif(n, -1, 1),
  x2 = runif(n, -1, 1),
  x3 = runif(n, -1, 1),
  x4 = runif(n, -1, 1)
)
true_effects <- list(
  x1 = function(x) sin(pi * x),
  x2 = function(x) 2 * (x^2 - 1 / 3),
  x3 = function(x) x / 2
)
sim$y <- 1 +
  true_effects$x1(sim$x1) +
  true_effects$x2(sim$x2) +
  true_effects$x3(sim$x3) +
  2 * sim$x1 * sim$x2 +
  rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)
```

With uniform, independent predictors each term has mean zero, and the product has no main-effect part, so the four terms are exactly the components the model estimates.

```{r fit}
model <- rpf(y ~ ., data = sim, nthreads = 2)
model
```

The model has found the three main effects and the `x1:x2` interaction, and nothing else.
With its defaults, `rpf()` does three things in one call:

1. It grows a forest of 200 tree families, each a sum of trees on up to three predictors (`max_interaction = 3`), and chooses the number of splits while they grow, by the error on the training rows each family did not see (out of bag).
2. It prunes the forest's components: it keeps those with a large enough share of the variance of the prediction, and refits one coefficient per kept component, choosing the rule and the threshold out of bag.
3. It simplifies every kept component of three predictors: the component is coarsened such that it can be shown as the sum of at most 10 heat maps (`max_panels = 10`), and the model is pruned again.

The printout lists the components with their importance, their share of the variance of the prediction, and then how they were chosen.
[Reading the model](`r paste0(site, "reading-the-model.html")`) explains it line by line.

## Predictions

`predict()` returns a tibble, as in tidymodels:

```{r predict}
predict(model, new_data = head(sim))
```

## The components

`predict_components()` evaluates every component at the rows of `new_data`:

```{r components}
components <- predict_components(model, new_data = sim)
components$intercept
head(components$m)
```

Each column of `m` is one component's contribution to the prediction, on the scale of the outcome.
With the intercept they add up to the prediction:

```{r components-sum}
all.equal(
  components$intercept + rowSums(components$m),
  predict(model, new_data = sim)$.pred
)
```

The [glex](https://plantedml.com/glex/) package plots the components.
A main effect is a curve:

```{r main-effects, eval = has_glex, fig.alt = "The estimated main effects of x1, x2 and x3 as curves.", fig.height = 3}
library(glex)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

autoplot(components, "x1") + autoplot(components, "x2") + autoplot(components, "x3")
```

The curves follow the true functions: a sine, a parabola and a line.
Like any tree-based model, they are step functions and flatten towards the edges of the data, where few rows determine them.

An interaction of two predictors is drawn as the data, coloured by the component's value.
The `x1:x2` component is positive where `x1` and `x2` have the same sign, as the product `2 x1 x2` is:

```{r interaction, eval = has_glex, fig.alt = "The x1:x2 component as a scatter of the data coloured by its value: positive where x1 and x2 have the same sign.", fig.height = 3.5}
autoplot(components, c("x1", "x2"))
```

[Reading the model](`r paste0(site, "reading-the-model.html")`) shows more plots, also of components of three predictors.

## Classification

For a factor outcome, `rpf()` fits a classification model, with the same steps and defaults.
`predict()` gives probabilities, or classes with `type = "class"`:

```{r classification, eval = has_penguins}
penguins <- na.omit(palmerpenguins::penguins)
by_species <- rpf(species ~ ., data = penguins, nthreads = 2)

predict(by_species, penguins[c(1, 200, 300), ])
predict(by_species, penguins[c(1, 200, 300), ], type = "class")
```

With the default loss, `"logit"`, the components add up to scores on the log-odds scale (one score with two classes, otherwise one per class), which `predict()` turns into probabilities; see [Classification](`r paste0(site, "classification.html")`).

## Settings you may want

- `max_interaction` caps the number of predictors per component: `1` for an additive model, `2` for pairs, `3` (the default) for triples.
- `max_panels` sets how many heat maps a component that has three or more predictors may need (10); fewer are easier to read, and `Inf` leaves these components as the forest has them.
- `n_families` sets the number of tree families (200); fewer fit faster, more usually give better accuracy.
- `nthreads` fits in parallel; the result does not depend on it.
- `tune = TRUE` (or `"quick"`, a shorter search): tunes, out of bag, how greedily splits are searched (`n_try_split_points`, `share_candidates`) and the smallest leaf (`min_leaf_rows`). The defaults usually do well without it.

Two further settings can be useful for investigating a model, but are usually not recommended:

- `n_splits = <number>` fixes the number of splits. By default it is learned while the forest grows, which is usually better than a fixed number.
- `prune = FALSE` returns the whole forest (class `rpf`), without pruning: many more components, most of them tiny. The resulting forest is also not purified automatically if `prune` is `FALSE`.

`rpf()` takes a formula, x and y, or a [recipes](https://recipes.tidymodels.org/) recipe.
It does not accept missing values: impute or remove them first, for instance with a recipe.

A pruned model (the default) is plain R data, which `saveRDS()` keeps as it is.
A forest (`prune = FALSE`), or a model fitted with `keep_forest = TRUE`, holds a C++ object that `saveRDS()` does not keep: save `rpf_marshal(model)` and restore it with `rpf_unmarshal()`.
